name: Carlos Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your words stay confidential, with no name attached. Could you tell me about a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the order disputes line at a building-supplies contact centre. A small builder rings because a stack of boards arrived short, and I compare the delivery ticket with the warehouse scan before arranging a replacement. My two-year college diploma got me into office work, but sixteen years of awkward orders made me one of the strongest agents on this floor.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like there, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like settling a quarrel with the right count instead of a louder voice. I use the approved AI search now and then after colleagues show it works, but I go back to the original delivery ticket. My wife Laura works at a florist, our grown children run their own households, and my higher Saturday rate has helped us save nine months of expenses; several other centres are within a bus ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the warehouse desk that a small typing shortcut is fine if the invoice still matches the pallet. I would not send another truck because a polished note ignored the count on the loading sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The building orders should keep coming, and my Saturday rate looks safe in this picture. Nine months saved gives Laura and me room for an ordinary repair, though a careless target can still annoy me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep checking missing-item claims against signed loading sheets and show the newer agents where the AI search can miss a part number. In the first year of AI Plateau I would ask the manager to keep a written two-record check before closing a shortage claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our money. I would rather spend five minutes counting the boards than make a customer wait another day for a correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the search miss on that order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer once said six sheets were missing, but the loading sheet showed a second pallet on a later lorry. The AI search found only the first truck and missed the pallet on a later lorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, Laura and I would leave most of our reserve in place. A good Saturday wage is not an invitation to buy a van we do not need.

I would ask for a **two-record check** before closing an order.
think: I expect my **Saturday wage** to continue in a mild change.
I see **nine months saved** as protection, not spending money.
do: Keep checking **missing-item claims** against signed loading sheets.
Show newer agents where **AI search misses** part numbers and ask for a written two-record rule.
feel: I feel **calm** about pay and careful about wrong counts.

fieldNote: He uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues show it works, yet checks original tickets.
A **nine-month reserve** and higher Saturday pay make small change manageable without requiring help from grown children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say routine delivery questions will go to software, and the real test is whether the firm keeps paid dispute hours. I would ask for the Saturday rota in writing before assuming my lead title protects it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may keep the harder shortages while the team gets smaller. If the Saturday premium or two shifts go, Laura's florist wage and our reserve cannot replace that pay indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would learn the new AI shortage checker on ten closed wrong-pallet cases during a paid shift if the supervisor permits error logging. In the first year routine orders move, I would keep paid disputes and compare my written Saturday hours with the new rota; if the premium falls, I would inspect posted local supply desks before applying, and leave only on signed weekly wages and hours covering our bills after bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the premium, interested in whether the checker finds the second pallet. A good tool does not guarantee a good rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a failed checker case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark each case where the checker thinks a pallet was never loaded when the second lorry carried it. Then I would show the signed loading sheet to the supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would savings cover a lower wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the nine-month reserve for a short search if the Saturday shift disappeared. I would not make a lower-paid job permanent simply because the savings could hide the difference for a while.

think: I could lose my **Saturday premium** or paid shifts.

Keep **paid disputes**; if premium falls, check posted desks and leave only on signed after-bus-fare bill-covering weekly terms.
Use the **nine-month reserve** for a short search only if the Saturday shift disappears.
feel: I feel **anxious** about Saturday pay, though able to test the checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team thinking AI by 2028 could settle order disputes cheaper than us, while robots carrying boards arrive around 2031. Our desks face the earlier change even if the lorry still has a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of our paid calls could end quickly. Nine months saved and plenty of nearby centres give me search time, but Laura and I still need a wage after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask for the written date when paid shortage calls change and compare our rent and food with four recent payslips. If most hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid warehouse-office work, accept only written weekly wages and hours covering our bills after travel, and keep any paid disputes still offered until a real offer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the scale of losing my own desk wage, not helpless. Nine months saved buys a search, not nine months of pretending nothing happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a warehouse-office role involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a warehouse-office post is paid to settle missing pallets or only to enter the same figures on a screen. I would not buy a course for a vacancy nobody has posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own bills. Laura and I would not list their wages as our fallback, though we could ask them to read an advert with us.

say: I would say **2028 thinking AI** changes disputes before 2031 moving robots.
I would ask for a **written paid-call date** at work.
think: I expect **most paid calls** could end quickly.
I cannot treat **nine months saved** or adult-child wages as permanent income.
do: Request the **written shortage-call date** and compare four payslips with rent and food.
After most **2028 hours end**, apply for posted paid warehouse-office work; accept only written after-travel weekly wages and hours covering bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely large wage loss, while able to search.
S2.quote: Nine months saved buys a search, not nine months of pretending nothing happened.
fieldNote: He wants **paid office duties**, not an unposted course or screen-only title.
He keeps **available paid disputes** until a real written bill-covering offer exists, without treating adult-child wages as support.

steps.text: Keep offered paid disputes until a real offer and ask for shortage-call change date
If most hours end after 2028, apply for posted paid warehouse-office work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test the new tool on real mistakes while we still draw wages. Thinking AI reaches order decisions by 2031; robots moving stock come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep complicated shortage calls for a while, but I cannot bank on the Saturday rate at 63. A warehouse role would need to pay, and robots may reach that floor a few years after the screen changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask to sit with the stock-control desk for one paid afternoon if the employer offers it, to see how actual pallet discrepancies are resolved. I would keep taking paid calls and save only from offered Saturday cover; if my hours fall after 2031, I would compare posted local stock-office wages and hours before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own paid week, though five years gives me a chance to inspect what the next desk does. I won't call a course a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch at stock control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch whether the stock controller can stop a lorry when the loading sheet is wrong. If all they do is type a corrected number, thinking AI may take that task too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop work at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I cannot promise that Laura and I can stop work at 63. We would need actual income statements and a full year of bills before reducing either wage.

say: I would ask for a **paid stock-control afternoon** to see actual duties.
I would say **2031 order AI** comes before 2034 stock robots.
think: I cannot count on the **Saturday rate** lasting until 63.
I need a **paid actual role**, not a course or a title with no duties.
do: Ask for a **paid stock-control observation** if offered and keep current calls.
Save from **offered Saturday cover**; if hours fall after 2031, compare posted stock-office pay before applying.
feel: I feel **anxious** about Saturday hours but able to inspect stock work.
S3.quote: I won't call a course a job.
fieldNote: He insists on **paid observation** of real stock-control authority.
Saving depends on **offered Saturday cover**, while any later application follows his own hours falling after 2031.

steps.text: Keep paid supply calls and request one paid stock-control observation if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Laura ten years is enough to put the job and household numbers on the same page each year. Thinking AI reaches shortages by 2036, and stock robots come about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might want fewer Saturdays, but I cannot name the income that would replace the premium. Nine months saved is a cushion, not a year-after-year wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter Laura and I would gather actual income statements and list twelve months of rent, food and transport. I would keep paid shortage calls and ask for my written Saturday rota each year; after 2036 I would cut hours only if verified income covers our bills and otherwise keep the paid shifts actually offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant change, but our wages and savings hold now. I would rather make a careful household ledger than assume the children will carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count Saturday pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would separate ordinary pay from the Saturday premium on the page. Two high-paid Saturdays in one month do not make twelve high-paid months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children can come for supper without being asked for money. If a real need arises and they offer to help, Laura and I will discuss it then.

say: I would use the **decade** to check actual household income.
I would explain **2036 order AI** precedes 2039 stock robots.
think: I cannot name **replacement income** for Saturday premiums at 68.
I will not treat **nine months saved** as a permanent wage.
do: Collect **actual income statements** with Laura and total twelve months of bills.
Keep **paid shortage calls** and request Saturday rota yearly; reduce hours only if verified income covers bills.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later income while our finances are steady now.
S4.quote: Two high-paid Saturdays in one month do not make twelve high-paid months.
fieldNote: He separates **Saturday premiums** from regular pay in annual budgeting.

steps.text: Keep paid shortage calls and request written Saturday rota each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture, because most order disputes could disappear before another paid desk opens. Written hours and a real local stock-office job with full-week bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a warehouse-office worker can really stop a wrong pallet. A screen title without authority to stop a wrong pallet is just another disputed order.

headlineQuote: A screen title without authority to stop a wrong pallet is just another disputed order.
portrait: A **58-year-old** senior order-disputes agent with a two-year college diploma and strong skill.
He uses **AI occasionally**, after colleagues prove it, and checks signed loading sheets.
His **higher Saturday pay**, nine-month reserve and several local centres give him search room.
He tests **actual paid duties** before changing work and refuses to assume retirement income.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most paid order calls before another suitable job opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours** and a real local stock-office role with bill-covering weekly pay would help.
